markers.title: The overdue notice names the report it came from
markers.finding: The safety team pointed out that a pile of hazard reports about the same thing, followed by an injury claim, documents poor housekeeping: reporting only helps if the fixes are recorded too (record ad-3).
markers.decision: The overdue notice names the hazard the action came from and the new incident on the same fryer, so an ageing action reads as risk rather than as admin.
markers.rejected: A plain count of overdue items with no link to the reports behind them.

markers.title: One step from the late action to the incident it now concerns
markers.finding: Where team members could not report directly, managers noted the basics on paper and entered everything at the end of the shift: double handling, and details got lost (record mf-8).
markers.decision: The notice links straight to the new incident, so the manager moves between the two records without re-keying a reference or searching the register.
markers.rejected: Making the manager find the incident by typing its reference into search.

markers.title: Lateness is on the card, in days
markers.finding: When incidents pile up the pressure is to close them quickly, which leads to shortcuts and reports closed without the proper steps (record fu-4).
markers.decision: Overdue actions carry a red edge and the number of days late beside the owner, so lateness is visible during a shift instead of surfacing in a monthly report.
markers.rejected: A separate overdue report, or an email digest that arrives after the fact.

markers.title: Every action carries the report it came from
markers.finding: Once a team member has told the manager, they have no visibility of what happens next or whether anything was logged (record aw-10).
markers.decision: Each card shows the reference of the report that produced it, so the system already knows who to tell when the action closes.
markers.rejected: A free-text task list kept apart from the reports, which is what left reporters with nothing to follow.

markers.title: A photo taken at the fix, not a memory test at sign-off
markers.finding: A manager described trying to resolve the issue on the spot and logging it afterwards, still recording the update (record ve-1).
markers.decision: Sign-off asks for one photo taken at the time of the fix, so the evidence is captured on the floor and the manager's step is a check rather than a reconstruction.
markers.rejected: A written close-out form with no evidence, which makes a quick close and a real fix look identical.

markers.title: Closed work stays on the board, quietly
markers.finding: A team member had seen logged hazards changed quickly, and that was why he kept reporting (record fu-5).
markers.decision: The closed column stays on the board for the whole period in a quieter, dashed treatment, so fixes remain in sight instead of disappearing the moment they are done.
markers.rejected: Hiding completed actions behind a filter, which is where the evidence of follow-through was being lost.

markers.title: Days to fix, not a count of reports
markers.finding: The safety team's view was that putting an incentive behind hazard identification makes everyone report one and the reports will not be real; the research proposed recognising outcomes instead (records fu-9, fu-11, aw-7).
markers.decision: Each closed card shows who reported it and how long the fix took, so the board measures outcomes rather than volume.
markers.rejected: A leaderboard of report counts, which the safety team warned would produce reports rather than fixes.

markers.title: The fixes notice prints from the board
markers.finding: The research proposed a poster or message each period listing what was fixed because someone reported it (record fu-12).
markers.decision: The notice is generated from the actions already closed on this board, so producing it costs a print rather than an evening of writing.
markers.rejected: A separately written monthly communication, which depends on someone having time to write it.
